TOXIC SNAKE PARK

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
With a (slowly) growing body of evidence linking heavy metal in the dust to disability and deformity Soweto activist Tiny Dlamini is waging a war to survival for the children of Snake Park

Unique Selling Point:
It’s surreal to walk through the rows of well-established informal homes in Snake Park and the small farming plots of Doornkop, sandwiched between Roodepoort and Dobsonville, Soweto with Tiny Dlamini. Animated, passionate, well-spoken and well-loved in this area, Tiny's trained eye can pick out every child with cerebral palsy (CP) and every animal with spinal deformity and skin disease. The overwhelming number of suffering children and animals begs an explanation.

We visit Snake Park on the day that French investigative filmmaker Martin Boudot presents findings from research that TV5 has just paid for -- a survey of the pollutants and chemicals that are found in Snake Park. Martin (who in 2016 released his investigation "Toxic Chemicals: Kids in Danger" on how our dependence of chemicals and pesticides harms children) has just spent 5 weeks in the the historic gold belt of Soweto and the West Rand to investigate the claims of deformity in animals, plants and birth defects in children.

In addition to French scientists that specialise in environmental toxicity (www.kudzuscience.com) Martin collaborated with our own AGRICULTURAL RESEARCH COUNCIL to sample and record the elevated levels of toxic chemicals in human and animal hair as well as in the water and soil from Snake Park and the other nearby hotspot Lancaster Dam, in the Wonderfontein Spruit area (in the same minings rights area as Snake Park).

TV5 spent over R120,000 on this research -- research that should be done routinely and should be informing epidemiological studies on a large scale in this area.

When Martin presented his findings to the Snake Park community who worked with him on his study, the BENCHMARKS FOUNDATION -- a think tank on global corporate responsibility with whom Tiny has teamed up to help establish scientific ground for her concerns -- handed out wheelchairs to the CP kids of Snake Park.

We filmed the disturbing picture of a community under siege by elements in their air, water and soil that they live with daily and from which there is no escape, nor for which they have any absolute explanations.

Martin's study (he can explain basics in Skype itv) and David van Wyk will explain possible consequences for residents, indicated that in the water samples there was:
Berillium that causes Intestinal lesions;
Chromium that causes Allergic dermatitis;
Nitrate -- infants below the age of six months who drink water containing nitrate in excess of the MCL could become seriously ill and, if untreated, may die. Symptoms include shortness of breath and blue-baby syndrome
Copper --Short term exposure: Gastrointestinal distress; Long term exposure: Liver or kidney damage;
Arsenic -- Skin damage or problems with circulatory systems, and may have increased risk of getting cancer
Selenium -- Hair or fingernail loss; numbness in fingers or toes; circulatory problems
Cadmium -- Kidney damage
Barium -- Increase in blood pressure
Mercury -- Kidney damage
Thalium -- Hair loss; changes in blood; kidney, intestine, or liver problems
Bishmuth -- Infants and children: Delays in physical or mental development; children could show slight deficits in attention span and learning abilities;
Adults: Kidney problems; high blood pressure
Uranium -- Increased risk of cancer, kidney toxicity

This is also an opportunity to report back on the WHO-backed research spearheaded by he FSE and Northwest University on uranium deposits in hair that we reported on in 2016 -- the study has faced some scientific hiccups that we will highlight -- but in the end it proved that uranium does find its way from mine tailings dust, through local water courses and soil into the body (not just from inhalation by miners, as was previously shown in Native American uranium mining communities) -- and so the FSE and academics are pressing on for the WHO to promote and/or fund and/or insist on epidemiological studies from our government.

With Tiny's help and that of her Benchmarks principal David van Wyk, we will also reflect on the Snake Park/Doornkop community is affected by the heavy metal toxicity of the environment as we attempt to extract accountability from the mines -- in this case DRDGold which has left wholly unrehabilitated, neglected, disintegrating dumps right next to Snake Park.

DRDGold is the historical miner, that Benchmarks holds responsible. But we also want to confront the current mining rights holder, MINTAILS (listed on the Austraian ASX) to whom the mining right for the area stretching from KRUGERSDORP TO JHB was sold/transferred by the Minister of Mineral Resources.

Astonishingly, just this week environmental management practitioners for WES WITS MINING (Australian Listed junior miner...but with "former" managers form DRD and Mintails) sent around information to the community and civil society that shows they intend to re-mine the dumps in this area even further.

The gold price is low because of the strength of the rand; most of the gold reserves are too deep to safely mine; Eskom has increased in electricity costs, the proposed carbon tax is a burden, the new mining charter looms, royalties are high -- all these factors are making of gold mining increasingly non-viable within the Witwatersrand. Other mines are downscaling (e.g. Anglo Gold Ashanti’s Tau Tona, Maponeng and Savuka Mines have been placed on care and maintenance). It therefore surprising and shocking to the community that West Wits Mining considers their project to be economically justifiable.

While walking around Snake Park with Tiny, we take Geiger counter readings -- in the area readings range from 20 to 27uSv/hr. A normal safe background reading for radiation varies roughly between 0.05-0.10.

DRDGold has vociferously defended its community engagement in SOME communities where Benchmarks have done research, but for Doornkop and Snake Park, there's no forum or ongoing engagement. DRDGold has denied their culpability an the conditions they've left behind. DGD says it "at some stage" fenced off and signposted old dumps -- but it put them at odds with a community where kids drown in the sinkholes of their unrehabilitated dumps. DRD's arrogance toward the community is quite staggering -- it has also said that dust from its mine dumps ‘pose no health risk and negligible public nuisance’, and that ‘there is no credible evidence that the dust is toxic’ -- but has not engaged with the high prevalence of respiratory illnesses in the communities studied by Benchmarks. According to Benchmarks research more than half (56.1%) of residents identified respiratory ailments (cough, sinus, asthma and TB) as their most persistent ailment. This is compared to only 25.6% of residents of Danville, Mafikeng, likewise identifying respiratory complaints. (Danville was chosen as a control study because it is a township with asbestos roofs that in all ways approximates Riverlea, except that there is no mining in close proximity.) DRD has been accused by a leading scientist of of using an outdated and outmoded system of dust measurement. DRD admits to a single leak from one of its pipelines in the vicinity of the Russell Stream in February 2016. Given that the company itself reported 16 environmental incidents in 2011 alone, this admission to a single incident in 2016 is quite remarkable. According to Dept of Water Affairs since 2014 two DRD operations were operating without water licences and ostensibly no applications for authorisation had been received by DWS.

MINTAILS has never even been hauled on the red carpet for the ongoing lack of rehabilitation now that they own the mining right -- it may be only about 10 years that the company has long been the target of the Human Rights Commission's investigations because it's essentially bankrupt and in business rescue. It holds the largest uranium reserved in the country but its gold mining has all but ground to a halt -- it just processes other small companies' ore.

Equally, we should approach the new mining minister Gwede Mantashe for comment -- as there has been no intervention to stop housing development and enforce mine closure and rehabilitation despite ongoing directives and court cases.

The health impact of mining pollution is not an easy story to understand and it's not an easy story to prove -- despite proof of elevated levels finding their way into human and animal bodies, the causal link to conditions like cancer and cerebral palsy and autism etc remains unproven.

Cerebral palsy (CP) is the most common motor disability in childhood. Population-based studies from around the world report prevalence estimates of CP ranging from 1.5 to more than 4 per 1,000 live births or children of a defined age range so while we can raise suspicions and ask questions, we will struggle to establish causation.

We will however speak to international experts who do research in highly industrialised mining areas, like India. About 1 in 323 children has been identified with CP according to estimates from America's CDC’s Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring (ADDM) Network. So it's up to us to work with local experts to try and put a figure on the prevalence in Snake Park.




Summary:
According to the peer reviewed REVIEW JOURNAL of AUTISM AND DEVELOPMENTAL DISORDERS, increasing evidence supports the role of industrial chemicals as contributors to the development of neurobehavioral disorders, including autism spectrum disorders, whose prevalence has progressively increased in recent years. Heavy metals, in particular, are recognized as neurodevelopmental toxins since they can be responsible of foetal damages which lead to neurological defects, developmental delays, learning disabilities and behavioral abnormalities. Most of the reviewed studies reported a relationship between exposure to metals during perinatal and early childhood periods and increased risk for autism. Moreover, the effects resulting from co-exposure to multiple metals should not be underestimated, especially in the assessment of children who live in developing countries or near heavily contaminated sites. Heavy metal contamination is one of the most severe threats for the environment and in unrehabilitated mining areas heavy metals in the environment occurs via a wide range of processes and pathways impacting on air, surface water, and soil quality. Due to the multiple sources of exposure, heavy metals represent also one of the most serious threats to human health (Arita and Costa 2009; Dufault et al. 2009; Szewczyk 2013). https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-014-0028-3

Even without the heavy concentration of poisonous mining compounds in the water, air and soil in one's immediate environment, city dwellers (all of us) are at risk of building up toxicity -- https://myersdetox.com/guide-sources-symptoms-toxic-metals/

BACKGROUND ON MINTAILS: https://www.businesslive.co.za/bd/companies/mining/2017-04-24-investor-willing-to-put-more-cash-into-mintailstroubled-mintails/

A long-standing investor in gold miner Mintails called Paige is willing to put more money into the company despite the litany of problems it faces, which have left shareholders of the Australian Securities Exchange-listed entity empty-handed.

Paige is a vehicle of the UK-based Harbour family, of which very little is known. Seager Rex Harbour owns City Securities and in the past was an active shareholder in a couple of other offshore mining companies, Medusa Mining and Maudore Minerals. He is also the founder of a UK charitable organisation called the Harbour Foundation.

Most of Mintails’ business is extracting gold from old dumps on the West Rand and toll treating material for other small gold miners at its Mogale Gold plants. It also has a small, shallow mine near Krugersdorp. It employs about 1,000 people, including contractors.

Mintails has faced periodic financial crises over the past decade and complaints about environmental damage.

The shares were suspended from trade in March 2015. In October 2015 Mintails Mining SA, Mintails Gold SA and Mintails Randfontein Cluster applied for business rescue.


According to the amended February business rescue plan drawn up by senior business rescue practitioner Dave Lake, contributing factors included technical problems with one of its two gold plants; overheads suitable for a bigger operation; a poor relationship with the Department of Mineral Resources, in particular over inadequate funding for its R336m of environmental liabilities; disputes among shareholders and management; accumulated liabilities; and lack of working capital.

The final trigger was a R20m bill from Eskom, which Mintails could not pay. Electricity is essential for it to be able to keep operating its treatment plants.

Mariette Liefferink, of the Federation for a Sustainable Environment, said the organisation laid a complaint with the South African Human Rights Commission alleging Mintails violated human rights on a number of grounds. These included its inadequate rehabilitation funding; ongoing pollution; failure to rehabilitate sites properly; contravention of the National Water Act; failure to comply with its environmental management plans; failure to rehabilitate the radioactive Tudor Dam and the nearby wetlands; and failures in managing the Lancaster Dam.

Liefferink said she was perplexed that Mintails’ R336m environmental liability was backed by only R16.8m in cash and guarantees, since mining companies were not allowed to start operations before they made full provision for environmental rehabilitation.

New management has been appointed and new black empowerment investors are being sought
Mintails claimed it rehabilitated as it processed dumps but this was only partly true, she said. In some areas it was making the problem worse, not better.

The law provided for directors and shareholders of a company to be held personally liable for environmental damage, she added.

The core of the 10-year recovery plan that Lake has proposed and creditors have agreed to is to raise the funding needed to restart gold plant two, refurbish gold plant one and fund the environmental liabilities over the life of operations, which is 20 years.

New, experienced management has already been appointed and new black empowerment investors are being sought.

Funds will come partly from the sale of assets, partly from a loan from Paige, subject to satisfactory due diligence, and partly from raising external loans, supported by Paige.

Lake declined to comment further on the plan at this stage.

Why the Harbour family would want to support Mintails, particularly given the possibility of environmental prosecution, is a mystery. But it has been invested for many years. In 2011 it made an unsuccessful A$80.6m ($60.75) takeover offer for Mintails and it has been supporting the business rescue process with post-commencement finance.

A company spokesman’s responses were vague when he was asked what merit Paige saw in Mintails, especially if it had to sell some of its gold tailings dumps, and why the entity was not deterred by its environmental liabilities.

He said Paige was working with the business rescue practitioner to save as many parts of the business as possible. Discussions were at a sensitive stage so he could not give more details on strategies or investments that have not been agreed.

It was important not to overstate the environmental liabilities, which were being tackled with the support of the Department of Mineral Resources, he said. "We remain very positive," he added.

Snake Park
Situated next to one of the world’s largest mine dumps, Snake Park near Soweto, is a community in distress with an unusually high number of Cerebral Palsy, respiratory diseases and inexplicable deformities in animals. With a growing body of evidence linking toxic dust in mine dumps to various illnesses in nearby communities, it appears environmental issues are to blame for these and other medical conditions. The circumstantial evidence is compelling, but there are still no empirical studies to make conclusive links. Carte Blanche searches for answers.



Script:


SCRIPT: TOXIC SNAKE PARK
PRODUCERS: Sinethemba Nogude & Anna-Maria van Niekerk
PRESENTER: Macfarlane Moleli
TX: 22 April 2018; DURATION: 10 minutes


The one place that single mother and activist Tiny Dlamini could afford to live when raising four kids was in Snake Park, where government-built homes extended with tin shacks, are squeezed in between old Soweto and a mine waste dump that’s been here for over a century -- they call it ‘The Mountain’.
TINY DLAMINI: Upon my arrival I realised this place was like no other. I realised everything here was not normal in terms of the environment. So, I’m a curious person, so I would examine the dust and I would wonder why this dust had white particles and realised there was something wrong with the dust.
INTRO LINK: Snake Park in Soweto has the unfortunate distinction of being located right next to the one of the world’s largest gold mine dumps -- but people’s relationship with their imposing neighbour is increasingly becoming uncomfortable.

Not far from the mine dump, Nobulawu Sitshaluza shares a shack with her 7-year old daughter Sinovuyo.
NOBULAWO SITSHALUSA: When it is autumn and gets windy, the mountain really wakes up, you can’t even see in front of you, when you walk in the street you can't see anything, you can’t see anybody. You can't hide from that dust. It gets through your pots, it gets in through your water. Sitting on a bed like this you see yourself being drawn.
Sinovuyo was born with Cerebral Palsy, CP for short -- a disorder that affects brain development, often causing problems with speaking, vision and muscle movement. Her mother says she is one of many.
NOBULAWO SITSHALUSA: There are quite a few in this area, there’s a child in this street, not far from me, the same street, there’s also a child I know of in Block 2, there’s a lot of kids like her...I came to be aware of that when Tiny was doing her programme...there are too many, sometimes you don’t even know how many there are but there are too many of these kids around.
Tiny suspect the dust brings with it disease, including CP.
TINY DLAMINI: You get people with TB, lung problems, you find people with silicosis and people with with sore eyes. As I was going house to house I came across children with these deformities...
Shocked by the sheer numbers of kids born with CP, and seeing that fear and stigma makes many parents keep kids hidden away, Snake Park resident Pontsho Madumo opened a care centre. With little to no funding she takes care of 17-year old Thabang and 11-year old Sinentlahla.
MAC: Pontsho were these kids also born in Snake Park?
PONTSHO MADUMO: Yes, they were born and raised here. There are a lot of kids here with disabilities. If you can check the orange files on the shelves, they are from when we used to have caregivers in the community going door to door, checking for kids with disabilities maybe twice a year.
MAC: How much does it take for you to take care of a child like this?
PONTSHO MADUMO: It’s extremely difficult to stay with these kids because we have an endless list of things we need, including beds, diapers and tissues.
The South African Chamber of Mines guideline is that people shouldn’t live closer than 500m from a mine dump. But collapsing in places, sand and water find their way into the the community -- seeping into soil where farmers like Jikile Sajini has seen a pig born with a deformed spine and his goats go blind.
JIKILE SAJINI: Their eyes turn brown and grey, they become blind and bump into everything.
MAC: I also heard that others have died, what happened?
JIKILE SAJINI: Those were the blind ones. When we slaughtered them it seemed like everything was ok, but the lungs were inflamed and had nodes all over them.
Tiny’s campaigning for answers...and for someone to fix the problem of the unattended dump.
TINY DLAMINI: No warning signs -- nothing, no one is taking responsibility. Children get swallowed by sinkholes, children swim there and are swallowed by the quicksand.
DAVID VAN WYK: (doing pool acid test) You can take it and bottle it, it it that clear...in fact it’s so acidic that nothing can live in it.
Tiny complained so loudly to local media that her cries reached the ears of David van Wyk, a sociologist and principal researcher for the Bench Marks Foundation. Funded by the South African Council of Churches, the NGO monitors the ethics of mining companies.
DAVID VAN WYK: As we stand here can you feel that it is hotter here than it was over there? It is heat from the materials and so on that is actually contained in the soil.
LINK: Mam Tiny calls it the silent killer, but exactly how this monster poisons the people, science has yet to confirm.
DAVID VAN WYK: We looked at Chernobyl in Russia and we also looked at India, okay? And… and what we discovered that there was a very, very close link between cerebral palsy and uranium, but it could also be caused by arsenic, it could also be caused by lead. If you ingest uranium, right, it can change your DNA codes and your DNA codes can scramble the way the kids come out.
All too easily mining companies and government are able to shrug off activists’ complaints, because no health studies have been done -- but the alarm bells were heard internationally. French science filmmaker Martin Boudot spent 5 weeks working with Tiny on a documentary on the plight of Joburg’s mine-affected communities.
MARTIN BOUDOT: Tiny is a hell of a woman, for sure. A situation like this in France will may make the headlines every day. We will never have the situation with so much environmental dangers very close from the populations…
Martin’s film will be broadcast in June to over a quarter of a billion people worldwide. As part of the film Martin did laboratory tests on hair samples of children and animals from Snake Park. He shared the findings with Tiny, fellow activists and some of the moms.
MARTIN BOUDOT: We analysed all these sample with the same spectrum -- heavy metals. Lead, it affects the brain, it affects different part of the bodies. We also found some cadmium, which is a carcinogenic element. We also found uranium. So we talk here about basically the worst chemicals on earth and they all are gathered in the same place and they are very poorly managed.
LINK: No-one wants to take responsibility for the dump -- the one owner passes it on to the next, the next passes it on to government. But the law is clear.
Government should only give licences if a mine has enough money saved in trust to close and fix the land after mining.
Here, historic owner DRDGOLD said they have no legal obligations anymore and they’d put measures in place to contain environmental impacts before selling to Mintails twelve years ago.
Mintails says DRDGOLD remains responsible until a new mining right is granted…which Mintails hasn’t not done as the company is still deciding what to do with these dumps -- market conditions make them not viable to mine.
Igor Klopcic, a mining geologist who’s worked with most big mining houses on the Witwatersrand attended the release of Martin’s results.
IGOR KLOPCIC: I do believe that dangers have been grossly underestimated and I’ll explain why. Danger from radioactive materials, especially loose ones like the mine dumps, comes from two different sources there are some materials on the mine dumps which are chemically poisonous. The second danger is gamma radiation which is radiation that affects you through your skin. Up to 300 metres away your body can be influenced by these gamma rays and it can cause damage to your tissue. There is a third danger which is the one that no one has yet spoken about, which is the danger of internal emitters, namely these are loose materials and if you pass nearby next to the mine dump or just…you could just live in Krugersdorp for example or Soweto. If you inhale mine dust you will have radioactive particles in your lungs. You could also swallow them. It contains radioactive particles which radiate cells in your lungs and can cause lung cancer.
Activist Mariette Liefferink’s Federation for a Sustainable Environment has campaigned for over a decade for credible science to prove the causal link between illness and mine waste -- so that government can ensure people are safe, as the Constitution provides.
MARIETTE: Unfortunately, there is a systemic non-enforcement of the non-compliance by some of the mining companies...in order for this matter to be taken forward, to escalate this matter there is an urgent need for a full epidemiological study or at least a health assessment.
LINK: Just in the two days I’ve been filming here in Snake Park, I felt a headache as soon as we got near these dumps -- but like with every report of eczema, asthma and especially cerebral palsy around here it will take immense political and moral will to get the kind of studies done that will give us the explanations we need.
For Tiny and the moms of Snake Park this can’t come any sooner. With nowhere to go, they are forced to coexist with the landmark.
NOBULAWO SITSHALUSA: I think as a parent, if you accept the situation you’re in, it becomes better, it’s a gift from God. They said she would die before attending school. I am grateful. Everything will get better in time.

Martin's study (he can explain basics in Skype itv) and David van Wyk will explain possible consequences for residents, indicated that in the water samples there was: Berillium that causes Intestinal lesions; Chromium that causes Allergic dermatitis; Nitrate -- infants below the age of six months who drink water containing nitrate in excess of the MCL could become seriously ill and, if untreated, may die. Symptoms include shortness of breath and blue-baby syndrome Copper --Short term exposure: Gastrointestinal distress; Long term exposure: Liver or kidney damage; Arsenic -- Skin damage or problems with circulatory systems, and may have increased risk of getting cancer Selenium -- Hair or fingernail loss; numbness in fingers or toes; circulatory problems Cadmium -- Kidney damage Barium -- Increase in blood pressure Mercury -- Kidney damage Thalium -- Hair loss; changes in blood; kidney, intestine, or liver problems Bishmuth -- Infants and children: Delays in physical or mental development; children could show slight deficits in attention span and learning abilities; Adults: Kidney problems; high blood pressure Uranium -- Increased risk of cancer, kidney toxicity This is also an opportunity to report back on the WHO-backed research spearheaded by he FSE and Northwest University on uranium deposits in hair that we reported on in 2016 -- the study has faced some scientific hiccups that we will highlight -- but in the end it proved that uranium does find its way from mine tailings dust, through local water courses and soil into the body (not just from inhalation by miners, as was previously shown in Native American uranium mining communities) -- and so the FSE and academics are pressing on for the WHO to promote and/or fund and/or insist on epidemiological studies from our government. With Tiny's help and that of her Benchmarks principal David van Wyk, we will also reflect on the Snake Park/Doornkop community is affected by the heavy metal toxicity of the environment as we attempt to extract accountability from the mines -- in this case DRDGold which has left wholly unrehabilitated, neglected, disintegrating dumps right next to Snake Park. DRDGold is the historical miner, that Benchmarks holds responsible. But we also want to confront the current mining rights holder, MINTAILS (listed on the Austraian ASX) to whom the mining right for the area stretching from KRUGERSDORP TO JHB was sold/transferred by the Minister of Mineral Resources. Astonishingly, just this week environmental management practitioners for WES WITS MINING (Australian Listed junior miner...but with "former" managers form DRD and Mintails) sent around information to the community and civil society that shows they intend to re-mine the dumps in this area even further. The gold price is low because of the strength of the rand; most of the gold reserves are too deep to safely mine; Eskom has increased in electricity costs, the proposed carbon tax is a burden, the new mining charter looms, royalties are high -- all these factors are making of gold mining increasingly non-viable within the Witwatersrand. Other mines are downscaling (e.g. Anglo Gold Ashanti’s Tau Tona, Maponeng and Savuka Mines have been placed on care and maintenance). It therefore surprising and shocking to the community that West Wits Mining considers their project to be economically justifiable. While walking around Snake Park with Tiny, we take Geiger counter readings -- in the area readings range from 20 to 27uSv/hr. A normal safe background reading for radiation varies roughly between 0.05-0.10. DRDGold has vociferously defended its community engagement in SOME communities where Benchmarks have done research, but for Doornkop and Snake Park, there's no forum or ongoing engagement. DRDGold has denied their culpability an the conditions they've left behind. DGD says it "at some stage" fenced off and signposted old dumps -- but it put them at odds with a community where kids drown in the sinkholes of their unrehabilitated dumps. DRD's arrogance toward the community is quite staggering -- it has also said that dust from its mine dumps ‘pose no health risk and negligible public nuisance’, and that ‘there is no credible evidence that the dust is toxic’ -- but has not engaged with the high prevalence of respiratory illnesses in the communities studied by Benchmarks. According to Benchmarks research more than half (56.1%) of residents identified respiratory ailments (cough, sinus, asthma and TB) as their most persistent ailment. This is compared to only 25.6% of residents of Danville, Mafikeng, likewise identifying respiratory complaints. (Danville was chosen as a control study because it is a township with asbestos roofs that in all ways approximates Riverlea, except that there is no mining in close proximity.) DRD has been accused by a leading scientist of of using an outdated and outmoded system of dust measurement. DRD admits to a single leak from one of its pipelines in the vicinity of the Russell Stream in February 2016. Given that the company itself reported 16 environmental incidents in 2011 alone, this admission to a single incident in 2016 is quite remarkable. According to Dept of Water Affairs since 2014 two DRD operations were operating without water licences and ostensibly no applications for authorisation had been received by DWS. MINTAILS has never even been hauled on the red carpet for the ongoing lack of rehabilitation now that they own the mining right -- it may be only about 10 years that the company has long been the target of the Human Rights Commission's investigations because it's essentially bankrupt and in business rescue. It holds the largest uranium reserved in the country but its gold mining has all but ground to a halt -- it just processes other small companies' ore. Equally, we should approach the new mining minister Gwede Mantashe for comment -- as there has been no intervention to stop housing development and enforce mine closure and rehabilitation despite ongoing directives and court cases. The health impact of mining pollution is not an easy story to understand and it's not an easy story to prove -- despite proof of elevated levels finding their way into human and animal bodies, the causal link to conditions like cancer and cerebral palsy and autism etc remains unproven. Cerebral palsy (CP) is the most common motor disability in childhood. Population-based studies from around the world report prevalence estimates of CP ranging from 1.5 to more than 4 per 1,000 live births or children of a defined age range so while we can raise suspicions and ask questions, we will struggle to establish causation. We will however speak to international experts who do research in highly industrialised mining areas, like India. About 1 in 323 children has been identified with CP according to estimates from America's CDC’s Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring (ADDM) Network. So it's up to us to work with local experts to try and put a figure on the prevalence in Snake Park. Summary: According to the peer reviewed REVIEW JOURNAL of AUTISM AND DEVELOPMENTAL DISORDERS, increasing evidence supports the role of industrial chemicals as contributors to the development of neurobehavioral disorders, including autism spectrum disorders, whose prevalence has progressively increased in recent years. Heavy metals, in particular, are recognized as neurodevelopmental toxins since they can be responsible of foetal damages which lead to neurological defects, developmental delays, learning disabilities and behavioral abnormalities. Most of the reviewed studies reported a relationship between exposure to metals during perinatal and early childhood periods and increased risk for autism. Moreover, the effects resulting from co-exposure to multiple metals should not be underestimated, especially in the assessment of children who live in developing countries or near heavily contaminated sites. Heavy metal contamination is one of the most severe threats for the environment and in unrehabilitated mining areas heavy metals in the environment occurs via a wide range of processes and pathways impacting on air, surface water, and soil quality. Due to the multiple sources of exposure, heavy metals represent also one of the most serious threats to human health (Arita and Costa 2009; Dufault et al. 2009; Szewczyk 2013). https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-014-0028-3 Even without the heavy concentration of poisonous mining compounds in the water, air and soil in one's immediate environment, city dwellers (all of us) are at risk of building up toxicity -- https://myersdetox.com/guide-sources-symptoms-toxic-metals/ Further information: BACKGROUND ON MINTAILS: https://www.businesslive.co.za/bd/companies/mining/2017-04-24-investor-willing-to-put-more-cash-into-mintailstroubled-mintails/ A long-standing investor in gold miner Mintails called Paige is willing to put more money into the company despite the litany of problems it faces, which have left shareholders of the Australian Securities Exchange-listed entity empty-handed. Paige is a vehicle of the UK-based Harbour family, of which very little is known. Seager Rex Harbour owns City Securities and in the past was an active shareholder in a couple of other offshore mining companies, Medusa Mining and Maudore Minerals. He is also the founder of a UK charitable organisation called the Harbour Foundation. Most of Mintails’ business is extracting gold from old dumps on the West Rand and toll treating material for other small gold miners at its Mogale Gold plants. It also has a small, shallow mine near Krugersdorp. It employs about 1,000 people, including contractors. Mintails has faced periodic financial crises over the past decade and complaints about environmental damage. The shares were suspended from trade in March 2015. In October 2015 Mintails Mining SA, Mintails Gold SA and Mintails Randfontein Cluster applied for business rescue. According to the amended February business rescue plan drawn up by senior business rescue practitioner Dave Lake, contributing factors included technical problems with one of its two gold plants; overheads suitable for a bigger operation; a poor relationship with the Department of Mineral Resources, in particular over inadequate funding for its R336m of environmental liabilities; disputes among shareholders and management; accumulated liabilities; and lack of working capital. The final trigger was a R20m bill from Eskom, which Mintails could not pay. Electricity is essential for it to be able to keep operating its treatment plants. Mariette Liefferink, of the Federation for a Sustainable Environment, said the organisation laid a complaint with the South African Human Rights Commission alleging Mintails violated human rights on a number of grounds. These included its inadequate rehabilitation funding; ongoing pollution; failure to rehabilitate sites properly; contravention of the National Water Act; failure to comply with its environmental management plans; failure to rehabilitate the radioactive Tudor Dam and the nearby wetlands; and failures in managing the Lancaster Dam. Liefferink said she was perplexed that Mintails’ R336m environmental liability was backed by only R16.8m in cash and guarantees, since mining companies were not allowed to start operations before they made full provision for environmental rehabilitation. New management has been appointed and new black empowerment investors are being sought Mintails claimed it rehabilitated as it processed dumps but this was only partly true, she said. In some areas it was making the problem worse, not better. The law provided for directors and shareholders of a company to be held personally liable for environmental damage, she added. The core of the 10-year recovery plan that Lake has proposed and creditors have agreed to is to raise the funding needed to restart gold plant two, refurbish gold plant one and fund the environmental liabilities over the life of operations, which is 20 years. New, experienced management has already been appointed and new black empowerment investors are being sought. Funds will come partly from the sale of assets, partly from a loan from Paige, subject to satisfactory due diligence, and partly from raising external loans, supported by Paige. Lake declined to comment further on the plan at this stage. Why the Harbour family would want to support Mintails, particularly given the possibility of environmental prosecution, is a mystery. But it has been invested for many years. In 2011 it made an unsuccessful A$80.6m ($60.75) takeover offer for Mintails and it has been supporting the business rescue process with post-commencement finance. A company spokesman’s responses were vague when he was asked what merit Paige saw in Mintails, especially if it had to sell some of its gold tailings dumps, and why the entity was not deterred by its environmental liabilities. He said Paige was working with the business rescue practitioner to save as many parts of the business as possible. Discussions were at a sensitive stage so he could not give more details on strategies or investments that have not been agreed. It was important not to overstate the environmental liabilities, which were being tackled with the support of the Department of Mineral Resources, he said. "We remain very positive," he added. Snake Park Situated next to one of the world’s largest mine dumps, Snake Park near Soweto, is a community in distress with an unusually high number of Cerebral Palsy, respiratory diseases and inexplicable deformities in animals. With a growing body of evidence linking toxic dust in mine dumps to various illnesses in nearby communities, it appears environmental issues are to blame for these and other medical conditions. The circumstantial evidence is compelling, but there are still no empirical studies to make conclusive links. Carte Blanche searches for answers. Script: SCRIPT: TOXIC SNAKE PARK PRODUCERS: Sinethemba Nogude & Anna-Maria van Niekerk PRESENTER: Macfarlane Moleli TX: 22 April 2018; DURATION: 10 minutes The one place that single mother and activist Tiny Dlamini could afford to live when raising four kids was in Snake Park, where government-built homes extended with tin shacks, are squeezed in between old Soweto and a mine waste dump that’s been here for over a century -- they call it ‘The Mountain’. TINY DLAMINI: Upon my arrival I realised this place was like no other. I realised everything here was not normal in terms of the environment. So, I’m a curious person, so I would examine the dust and I would wonder why this dust had white particles and realised there was something wrong with the dust. INTRO LINK: Snake Park in Soweto has the unfortunate distinction of being located right next to the one of the world’s largest gold mine dumps -- but people’s relationship with their imposing neighbour is increasingly becoming uncomfortable. Not far from the mine dump, Nobulawu Sitshaluza shares a shack with her 7-year old daughter Sinovuyo. NOBULAWO SITSHALUSA: When it is autumn and gets windy, the mountain really wakes up, you can’t even see in front of you, when you walk in the street you can't see anything, you can’t see anybody. You can't hide from that dust. It gets through your pots, it gets in through your water. Sitting on a bed like this you see yourself being drawn. Sinovuyo was born with Cerebral Palsy, CP for short -- a disorder that affects brain development, often causing problems with speaking, vision and muscle movement. Her mother says she is one of many. NOBULAWO SITSHALUSA: There are quite a few in this area, there’s a child in this street, not far from me, the same street, there’s also a child I know of in Block 2, there’s a lot of kids like her...I came to be aware of that when Tiny was doing her programme...there are too many, sometimes you don’t even know how many there are but there are too many of these kids around. Tiny suspect the dust brings with it disease, including CP. TINY DLAMINI: You get people with TB, lung problems, you find people with silicosis and people with with sore eyes. As I was going house to house I came across children with these deformities... Shocked by the sheer numbers of kids born with CP, and seeing that fear and stigma makes many parents keep kids hidden away, Snake Park resident Pontsho Madumo opened a care centre. With little to no funding she takes care of 17-year old Thabang and 11-year old Sinentlahla. MAC: Pontsho were these kids also born in Snake Park? PONTSHO MADUMO: Yes, they were born and raised here. There are a lot of kids here with disabilities. If you can check the orange files on the shelves, they are from when we used to have caregivers in the community going door to door, checking for kids with disabilities maybe twice a year. MAC: How much does it take for you to take care of a child like this? PONTSHO MADUMO: It’s extremely difficult to stay with these kids because we have an endless list of things we need, including beds, diapers and tissues. The South African Chamber of Mines guideline is that people shouldn’t live closer than 500m from a mine dump. But collapsing in places, sand and water find their way into the the community -- seeping into soil where farmers like Jikile Sajini has seen a pig born with a deformed spine and his goats go blind. JIKILE SAJINI: Their eyes turn brown and grey, they become blind and bump into everything. MAC: I also heard that others have died, what happened? JIKILE SAJINI: Those were the blind ones. When we slaughtered them it seemed like everything was ok, but the lungs were inflamed and had nodes all over them. Tiny’s campaigning for answers...and for someone to fix the problem of the unattended dump. TINY DLAMINI: No warning signs -- nothing, no one is taking responsibility. Children get swallowed by sinkholes, children swim there and are swallowed by the quicksand. DAVID VAN WYK: (doing pool acid test) You can take it and bottle it, it it that clear...in fact it’s so acidic that nothing can live in it. Tiny complained so loudly to local media that her cries reached the ears of David van Wyk, a sociologist and principal researcher for the Bench Marks Foundation. Funded by the South African Council of Churches, the NGO monitors the ethics of mining companies. DAVID VAN WYK: As we stand here can you feel that it is hotter here than it was over there? It is heat from the materials and so on that is actually contained in the soil. LINK: Mam Tiny calls it the silent killer, but exactly how this monster poisons the people, science has yet to confirm. DAVID VAN WYK: We looked at Chernobyl in Russia and we also looked at India, okay? And… and what we discovered that there was a very, very close link between cerebral palsy and uranium, but it could also be caused by arsenic, it could also be caused by lead. If you ingest uranium, right, it can change your DNA codes and your DNA codes can scramble the way the kids come out. All too easily mining companies and government are able to shrug off activists’ complaints, because no health studies have been done -- but the alarm bells were heard internationally. French science filmmaker Martin Boudot spent 5 weeks working with Tiny on a documentary on the plight of Joburg’s mine-affected communities. MARTIN BOUDOT: Tiny is a hell of a woman, for sure. A situation like this in France will may make the headlines every day. We will never have the situation with so much environmental dangers very close from the populations… Martin’s film will be broadcast in June to over a quarter of a billion people worldwide. As part of the film Martin did laboratory tests on hair samples of children and animals from Snake Park. He shared the findings with Tiny, fellow activists and some of the moms. MARTIN BOUDOT: We analysed all these sample with the same spectrum -- heavy metals. Lead, it affects the brain, it affects different part of the bodies. We also found some cadmium, which is a carcinogenic element. We also found uranium. So we talk here about basically the worst chemicals on earth and they all are gathered in the same place and they are very poorly managed. LINK: No-one wants to take responsibility for the dump -- the one owner passes it on to the next, the next passes it on to government. But the law is clear. Government should only give licences if a mine has enough money saved in trust to close and fix the land after mining. Here, historic owner DRDGOLD said they have no legal obligations anymore and they’d put measures in place to contain environmental impacts before selling to Mintails twelve years ago. Mintails says DRDGOLD remains responsible until a new mining right is granted…which Mintails hasn’t not done as the company is still deciding what to do with these dumps -- market conditions make them not viable to mine. Igor Klopcic, a mining geologist who’s worked with most big mining houses on the Witwatersrand attended the release of Martin’s results. IGOR KLOPCIC: I do believe that dangers have been grossly underestimated and I’ll explain why. Danger from radioactive materials, especially loose ones like the mine dumps, comes from two different sources there are some materials on the mine dumps which are chemically poisonous. The second danger is gamma radiation which is radiation that affects you through your skin. Up to 300 metres away your body can be influenced by these gamma rays and it can cause damage to your tissue. There is a third danger which is the one that no one has yet spoken about, which is the danger of internal emitters, namely these are loose materials and if you pass nearby next to the mine dump or just…you could just live in Krugersdorp for example or Soweto. If you inhale mine dust you will have radioactive particles in your lungs. You could also swallow them. It contains radioactive particles which radiate cells in your lungs and can cause lung cancer. Activist Mariette Liefferink’s Federation for a Sustainable Environment has campaigned for over a decade for credible science to prove the causal link between illness and mine waste -- so that government can ensure people are safe, as the Constitution provides. MARIETTE: Unfortunately, there is a systemic non-enforcement of the non-compliance by some of the mining companies...in order for this matter to be taken forward, to escalate this matter there is an urgent need for a full epidemiological study or at least a health assessment. LINK: Just in the two days I’ve been filming here in Snake Park, I felt a headache as soon as we got near these dumps -- but like with every report of eczema, asthma and especially cerebral palsy around here it will take immense political and moral will to get the kind of studies done that will give us the explanations we need. For Tiny and the moms of Snake Park this can’t come any sooner. With nowhere to go, they are forced to coexist with the landmark. NOBULAWO SITSHALUSA: I think as a parent, if you accept the situation you’re in, it becomes better, it’s a gift from God. They said she would die before attending school. I am grateful. According to Benchmarks research more than half (56.1%) of residents identified respiratory ailments (cough, sinus, asthma and TB) as their most persistent ailment. This is compared to only 25.6% of residents of Danville, Mafikeng, likewise identifying respiratory complaints. (Danville was chosen as a control study because it is a township with asbestos roofs that in all ways approximates Riverlea, except that there is no mining in close proximity.) DRD has been accused by a leading scientist of of using an outdated and outmoded system of dust measurement. DRD admits to a single leak from one of its pipelines in the vicinity of the Russell Stream in February 2016. Given that the company itself reported 16 environmental incidents in 2011 alone, this admission to a single incident in 2016 is quite remarkable. According to Dept of Water Affairs since 2014 two DRD operations were operating without water licences and ostensibly no applications for authorisation had been received by DWS. MINTAILS has never even been hauled on the red carpet for the ongoing lack of rehabilitation now that they own the mining right -- it may be only about 10 years that the company has long been the target of the Human Rights Commission's investigations because it's essentially bankrupt and in business rescue. It holds the largest uranium reserved in the country but its gold mining has all but ground to a halt -- it just processes other small companies' ore. Equally, we should approach the new mining minister Gwede Mantashe for comment -- as there has been no intervention to stop housing development and enforce mine closure and rehabilitation despite ongoing directives and court cases. The health impact of mining pollution is not an easy story to understand and it's not an easy story to prove -- despite proof of elevated levels finding their way into human and animal bodies, the causal link to conditions like cancer and cerebral palsy and autism etc remains unproven. Cerebral palsy (CP) is the most common motor disability in childhood. Population-based studies from around the world report prevalence estimates of CP ranging from 1.5 to more than 4 per 1,000 live births or children of a defined age range so while we can raise suspicions and ask questions, we will struggle to establish causation. We will however speak to international experts who do research in highly industrialised mining areas, like India. About 1 in 323 children has been identified with CP according to estimates from America's CDC’s Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring (ADDM) Network. So it's up to us to work with local experts to try and put a figure on the prevalence in Snake Park.
metadata.Summary: According to the peer reviewed REVIEW JOURNAL of AUTISM AND DEVELOPMENTAL DISORDERS, increasing evidence supports the role of industrial chemicals as contributors to the development of neurobehavioral disorders, including autism spectrum disorders, whose prevalence has progressively increased in recent years. Heavy metals, in particular, are recognized as neurodevelopmental toxins since they can be responsible of foetal damages which lead to neurological defects, developmental delays, learning disabilities and behavioral abnormalities. Most of the reviewed studies reported a relationship between exposure to metals during perinatal and early childhood periods and increased risk for autism. Moreover, the effects resulting from co-exposure to multiple metals should not be underestimated, especially in the assessment of children who live in developing countries or near heavily contaminated sites. Heavy metal contamination is one of the most severe threats for the environment and in unrehabilitated mining areas heavy metals in the environment occurs via a wide range of processes and pathways impacting on air, surface water, and soil quality. Due to the multiple sources of exposure, heavy metals represent also one of the most serious threats to human health (Arita and Costa 2009; Dufault et al. 2009; Szewczyk 2013). https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-014-0028-3 Even without the heavy concentration of poisonous mining compounds in the water, air and soil in one's immediate environment, city dwellers (all of us) are at risk of building up toxicity -- https://myersdetox.com/guide-sources-symptoms-toxic-metals/
metadata.Further information: BACKGROUND ON MINTAILS: https://www.businesslive.co.za/bd/companies/mining/2017-04-24-investor-willing-to-put-more-cash-into-mintailstroubled-mintails/ A long-standing investor in gold miner Mintails called Paige is willing to put more money into the company despite the litany of problems it faces, which have left shareholders of the Australian Securities Exchange-listed entity empty-handed. Paige is a vehicle of the UK-based Harbour family, of which very little is known. Seager Rex Harbour owns City Securities and in the past was an active shareholder in a couple of other offshore mining companies, Medusa Mining and Maudore Minerals. He is also the founder of a UK charitable organisation called the Harbour Foundation. Most of Mintails’ business is extracting gold from old dumps on the West Rand and toll treating material for other small gold miners at its Mogale Gold plants. It also has a small, shallow mine near Krugersdorp. It employs about 1,000 people, including contractors. Mintails has faced periodic financial crises over the past decade and complaints about environmental damage. The shares were suspended from trade in March 2015. In October 2015 Mintails Mining SA, Mintails Gold SA and Mintails Randfontein Cluster applied for business rescue. According to the amended February business rescue plan drawn up by senior business rescue practitioner Dave Lake, contributing factors included technical problems with one of its two gold plants; overheads suitable for a bigger operation; a poor relationship with the Department of Mineral Resources, in particular over inadequate funding for its R336m of environmental liabilities; disputes among shareholders and management; accumulated liabilities; and lack of working capital. The final trigger was a R20m bill from Eskom, which Mintails could not pay. Electricity is essential for it to be able to keep operating its treatment plants. Mariette Liefferink, of the Federation for a Sustainable Environment, said the organisation laid a complaint with the South African Human Rights Commission alleging Mintails violated human rights on a number of grounds. These included its inadequate rehabilitation funding; ongoing pollution; failure to rehabilitate sites properly; contravention of the National Water Act; failure to comply with its environmental management plans; failure to rehabilitate the radioactive Tudor Dam and the nearby wetlands; and failures in managing the Lancaster Dam. Liefferink said she was perplexed that Mintails’ R336m environmental liability was backed by only R16.8m in cash and guarantees, since mining companies were not allowed to start operations before they made full provision for environmental rehabilitation. New management has been appointed and new black empowerment investors are being sought Mintails claimed it rehabilitated as it processed dumps but this was only partly true, she said. In some areas it was making the problem worse, not better. The law provided for directors and shareholders of a company to be held personally liable for environmental damage, she added. The core of the 10-year recovery plan that Lake has proposed and creditors have agreed to is to raise the funding needed to restart gold plant two, refurbish gold plant one and fund the environmental liabilities over the life of operations, which is 20 years. New, experienced management has already been appointed and new black empowerment investors are being sought. Funds will come partly from the sale of assets, partly from a loan from Paige, subject to satisfactory due diligence, and partly from raising external loans, supported by Paige. Lake declined to comment further on the plan at this stage. Why the Harbour family would want to support Mintails, particularly given the possibility of environmental prosecution, is a mystery. But it has been invested for many years. In 2011 it made an unsuccessful A$80.6m ($60.75) takeover offer for Mintails and it has been supporting the business rescue process with post-commencement finance. A company spokesman’s responses were vague when he was asked what merit Paige saw in Mintails, especially if it had to sell some of its gold tailings dumps, and why the entity was not deterred by its environmental liabilities. He said Paige was working with the business rescue practitioner to save as many parts of the business as possible. Discussions were at a sensitive stage so he could not give more details on strategies or investments that have not been agreed. It was important not to overstate the environmental liabilities, which were being tackled with the support of the Department of Mineral Resources, he said. "We remain very positive," he added.
